rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The elution window will guide subsequent solvent-window and slope adjustments.

Injection 1 already attained the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure the critical pair’s slope sensitivity.

The critical pair responds strongly to gradient slope, falling below the resolution target at 6 minutes. Test the intermediate 8-minute gradient to recover full resolution with a shorter elution time than injection 1.

The 8-minute gradient retains maximum CRF with a small resolution margin. Raise temperature while keeping the gradient unchanged to test whether faster elution and altered selectivity preserve full resolution.

Trim the solvent window and shorten the gradient while keeping its slope close to the fully resolved 8-minute run at 50 C. Starting below the first peak’s estimated elution composition should reduce early waiting time while preserving useful separation.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten elution further. Keeping the endpoint fixed makes the gradient slightly shallower, which may protect the critical pair’s small resolution margin; monitor early-pair compression as well.

Test a narrower, 4-minute gradient to reduce elution time while slightly lowering the slope to support the critical pair. The main risk is compression of the earliest peaks as the starting organic fraction increases.

Lower the endpoint one step to make the gradient shallower and recover resolution of the critical middle pair. The last peak previously eluted near 0.50 organic, so a 0.60 endpoint should still elute all six compounds promptly.

Test a much steeper gradient to see whether the critical middle pair crosses elution order and separates again, potentially yielding a substantially faster method. Restore the low starting organic fraction to protect early-peak retention during this exploratory run.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves middle-pair selectivity in the fast-gradient regime while shortening elution further. Keep temperature fixed to isolate the solvent-window effect, watching for early-peak compression.

Lower temperature to probe selectivity of the unresolved middle pair in the fast-gradient regime, where elution order may differ from the slower runs. Holding the gradient fixed isolates the temperature effect while retaining a short expected elution time.

Return to a shallow gradient and test whether a higher starting organic fraction can shorten the fully resolved method. Lowering temperature relative to injection 8 should help retain the earliest peaks, while the narrower solvent window supports middle-pair resolution.

Test a 4-minute gradient with a slope between injections 5 and 6, both fully resolved. This may preserve the critical pair at R ≥ 1.5 while slightly reducing the last-peak time relative to injection 8.

Raise temperature one step to try to lift the critical middle pair above R = 1.5 while shortening elution. Earlier temperature results suggest improved middle-pair selectivity, but the first pair must be monitored because its resolution decreases with temperature.

Return to 50 C to restore early-pair resolution and lower the endpoint to recover the middle pair through a shallower gradient. This tests a more robust maximum-CRF alternative to injection 8 while keeping elution comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test whether lowering the starting organic fraction restores the early-pair resolution lost at 55 C. The gradient slope matches injection 14, helping distinguish the starting-composition effect while retaining temperature’s benefit to middle-pair selectivity.

Refine around injection 8, the fastest fully resolved result, with a slightly shallower gradient to increase its narrow middle-pair resolution margin. This should preserve maximum CRF with only a modest increase in elution time.

Maximum CRF is already secured; test a slightly shallower version of injection 15 to improve the minimum-resolution margin. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so all six compounds should still elute well within 10 minutes.

Test a gradient slope between the fully resolved injection 8 and the faster but under-resolved injection 7. This fine grid adjustment may shorten the last-peak time while keeping the critical middle pair at R ≥ 1.5.

Test a 2-minute narrow gradient whose shallow slope should preserve the critical middle-pair separation, followed by elution of later peaks during the hold. The lower endpoint may extend last-peak time, but this explores whether full resolution can be retained with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a lower-temperature alternative near the fastest fully resolved method, using a shallower gradient to compensate for reduced middle-pair selectivity. This may provide stronger early-pair resolution while retaining maximum CRF and a short elution time.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 21 to shorten elution, using its middle-pair resolution margin. Comparison with injection 8 will also show whether the fastest fully resolved gradient remains resolved at 5 C lower temperature.

Test the temperature tolerance of injection 15, which had more resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method. Lowering temperature should improve early-pair separation; the key question is whether the middle pair remains above R = 1.5.

Refine around injection 8 by lowering the endpoint one step to strengthen middle-pair resolution while retaining its adequate early-pair separation. This should offer a maximum-CRF alternative with more resolution margin and faster elution than injection 21.

Use a slope between injections 21 and 22 to seek a faster fully resolved method at 45 C, where early-pair resolution is stronger than at 50 C. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
